text: Credential Guard and LSA Protection — two real Windows controls that stop credential theft through genuinely different mechanisms, even once an attacker already has administrative code running on the box. Knowing what each one actually protects, and what it depends on, matters more than just flipping both on.

Credential Guard isn't available on anything. It needs a 64-bit CPU with virtualization extensions and Second Level Address Translation, UEFI firmware with Secure Boot enabled, and Windows Enterprise or Education — not Home or Pro. A TPM 2.0 chip is recommended for stronger key protection, and every boot driver on the machine has to tolerate running underneath the Hyper-V hypervisor layer, since Virtualization-Based Security uses that layer even when the Hyper-V role is never installed.

Credential Guard runs an isolated process called LSAIso.exe inside that hypervisor-protected container, separate from the main kernel. The regular lsass.exe still runs, but it no longer holds the raw NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets itself — it asks the isolated process to do that work. LSA Protection is a separate setting entirely: RunAsPPL makes lsass.exe a Protected Process Light, so only signed, trusted code can load into it, with a value of 2 running it in audit mode first to catch incompatible drivers before full enforcement.

Put the two together and a real credential-dumping attempt fails twice over. Credential Guard means the secrets a tool like Mimikatz goes looking for were never in lsass.exe's own memory to begin with, even for an attacker with local administrator rights. LSA Protection means the attempt to inject Mimikatz's module into lsass.exe in the first place gets refused, because that process now only accepts signed code.

Two different mechanisms, stopping two different steps of the same well-known attack technique — which is exactly why both get deployed together rather than treated as interchangeable, and exactly why an engineer should know which control stopped the attempt when a tabletop exercise or a real incident asks. Next up: measuring whether hardening like this actually worked, instead of assuming it did the moment a GPO gets linked.
